title: Start with the bill
say: Every month, the average Airtel mobile customer pays two hundred and seventy one rupees. A year ago, it was two hundred and fifty six.

title: Start with the bill
say: So who raised it? The price? The plan? Or the customer's reluctance to leave?

title: Name the question
say: That number is called ARPU: average revenue per user, per month. Airtel reports it for its Indian mobile business, from three hundred and seventy seven million customers.

title: Name the question
say: A telecom moat can come from three places. Scale: a vast network shared by many customers. Switching costs: it hurts to leave. And pricing power: you can charge more, and customers stay.

title: Name the question
say: Airtel's pitch is the second one. It says bundling mobile, broadband and TV, what it calls convergence, makes customers stickier. So we tested that against the filings.

title: Name the question
say: Not against opinions. Against Airtel's own results, its rivals' filings, and the regulator's data. Where the data cannot answer, we will say so.

title: The line itself
say: Start with the line. In September twenty twenty four, ARPU was two hundred and thirty three rupees. Today, two hundred and seventy one. Sixteen percent more, over eight quarters of change.

title: The line itself
say: It did not rise in a straight line. It stayed at two hundred and forty five for two quarters, and slipped in the March twenty twenty six quarter before climbing again.

title: The line itself
say: Now split the growth. Mobile revenue is up ten percent on last year. The customer base is up three point six percent. ARPU is up five point nine.

title: The line itself
say: So, very roughly, three-fifths of the extra revenue comes from each customer paying more, and two-fifths from having more customers. That is our simplification, not Airtel's. And customer additions are slowing: seven hundred and sixteen thousand this quarter, against three point three million in June.

title: The line itself
say: One more caution. Management says both last quarter's two hundred and sixty four and this quarter's two hundred and seventy one had the benefit of an extra day. So the quarter-to-quarter climb is less steep than it looks.

title: Suspect one: price
say: Suspect one: price. Airtel's filings show no dated tariff increase. But in Airtel's own recording of this quarter's call, management says it took a pricing intervention, and that it has played out. It also says a move like that always has a temporary effect on customers staying.

title: Suspect one: price
say: But ARPU was rising before this move. In its earlier calls, management said it was growing ARPU in the absence of any tariff repair, through upgrades, data and roaming. And it does not say how much of the lift comes from the new move.

title: Suspect one: price
say: So price is a real suspect, but not the only one. The filings cannot say how much it explains.

title: Suspect two: postpaid
say: Suspect two: postpaid. Airtel added one point two million postpaid customers this quarter, which it calls its best ever, taking the base to thirty one point two million.

title: Suspect two: postpaid
say: That sounds large. But postpaid is still only eight point three percent of its mobile customers. A year ago, seven point six.

title: Suspect two: postpaid
say: Airtel does not disclose postpaid ARPU, so we cannot say how much more a postpaid customer pays, or how much of its ARPU comes from them. So mix may be helping, and by how much is not something the filings say.

title: Suspect three: convergence
say: Suspect three: convergence. This is the big bet. Airtel's home broadband and fibre business now has fifteen point four million customers, three point four million more than a year ago. It is adding homes more slowly, though: six hundred and seventy six thousand this quarter, against nine hundred and fifty one thousand a year ago.

title: Suspect three: convergence
say: Management says that when a customer has both Wi-Fi and mobile, their churn, the rate at which they leave, drops by nearly fifty percent. It gave no base for that number. In the next quarter's call, management said convergence will be an important lever.

title: Suspect three: convergence
say: So the question is whether those fifteen million homes are paying for the bet. Let us look at what they earn.

title: What the homes earn
say: Homes revenue this quarter: two thousand three hundred and thirty six crore rupees. Profit before interest and tax: one hundred and fifty seven crore. A margin of six point seven percent. A year ago, sixteen point two.

title: What the homes earn
say: Revenue per home has fallen every quarter for two years. From five hundred and sixty six rupees to five hundred and nine. Ten percent lower, while in the last year alone the number of homes grew by more than a quarter. On this quarter's call, management says the latest fall is a one-off, a carry-over from low-priced sales it corrected last quarter.

title: What the homes earn
say: And the business spent two thousand one hundred and eighty one crore on capex in the quarter. Its EBITDA was one thousand one hundred and forty crore. So, after capex, about one thousand and forty one crore more went out than came in.

title: What the homes earn
say: Airtel itself says its share of homes is, in the long term, a very significant moat. Maybe. But so far, the numbers we can see show an investment, not yet a return.

title: Does stickiness show?
say: If customers were stickier, churn should be falling. Airtel's monthly mobile churn is two point nine percent. A year ago, also two point nine. Last quarter, two point six. Management says this quarter's churn reflects seasonality and the pricing move, and that the pricing effect is temporary. We cannot test that yet.

title: Does stickiness show?
say: Management also says the fast growth in fixed-wireless homes brought higher churn in some customer groups, and that it tightened the quality of its sales.

title: Does stickiness show?
say: Digital TV, the third leg of the bundle, lost four hundred and forty three thousand customers this quarter, at a loss of about one hundred and thirty two crore rupees. Its monthly churn is three point five percent.

title: Scale and share
say: What about scale? The regulator's September data puts Jio at thirty nine point three percent of mobile connections, and Airtel at thirty eight. Airtel edged up from June.

title: Scale and share
say: But Airtel's count includes eighty nine million machine-to-machine connections, sixty one percent of all of them in India. Take those out, and Airtel has about thirty five percent of ordinary mobile connections. Jio, about forty two.

title: Scale and share
say: Measured by active share, the share of connections actually in use, the two are level: about ninety nine percent each.

title: Scale and share
say: So scale is real. The headline flatters Airtel a little.

title: What the balance sheet buys
say: The money side gives Airtel time. For the whole group, including Africa, net debt, including lease obligations, is about one point two times a year's EBITDA, down from about one point six a year ago. Return on capital is twenty three percent, up from nineteen.

title: What the balance sheet buys
say: It is also investing heavily. Capex was twelve thousand four hundred and sixty seven crore rupees, plus two thousand eight hundred and twenty six crore for land for data centres, which Airtel reports separately. Net finance costs rose to five thousand and fifty eight crore, from four thousand four hundred and twenty eight.

title: What the balance sheet buys
say: Net income before one-off items rose thirty three percent, to nine thousand and fifteen crore rupees. We leave out a comparison with Jio's margin. The two companies measure it on different bases.

title: Return to the bill
say: So, which suspect is it? Our arithmetic says ARPU explains about three-fifths of the growth in mobile revenue, but Airtel does not say how much of that is price. Postpaid is real, and small. Convergence is large in homes, not yet paying in the money, and its main promised benefit, lower churn, is a claim without a base.

title: Return to the bill
say: Our view, as analysis and not a filing fact: today, Airtel's moat shows more in pricing and scale than in proven stickiness. Another reading is also fair: convergence may be an investment whose payoff comes later.

title: Return to the bill
say: Four things will settle it. Churn. Revenue and margin per home. The next tariff move. And Airtel's own filed transcript of this quarter's call, to check the wording.

title: Return to the bill
say: Two hundred and seventy one rupees a month. Convergence is meant to protect it. The filings show ARPU lifting it. They do not say how much is price.
